The Jackal buzzard (Buteo rufofuscus) is a medium-sized raptor endemic to southern Africa, where it inhabits montane grasslands and rocky escarpments. Field studies indicate that newly hatched chicks emerge from eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] after an incubation period of approximately 39.5 days [ab = approximately 39.5 days], a duration consistent with the extended developmental time characteristic of large-bodied Buteo species. At hatching, these altricial nestlings weigh a mere 30 grams [Wwb = 30 grams], a modest initial mass that underscores the substantial parental investment required during the subsequent brooding and provisioning phases. This low birth weight contrasts sharply with the adult body sizes achieved later in life, reflecting a pronounced growth trajectory typical of top-order avian predators in resource-limited environments.

Adult females attain a maximum body mass of approximately 1330 grams [Wwi = approximately 1330 grams], whereas conspecific males plateau at a comparatively lower 988 grams [Wwi = 988 grams]. This dimorphism, likely driven by the energetic demands of egg production and incubation in females, follows patterns seen in other accipitrid raptors where the larger sex assumes a greater share of nest defense and brooding duties. The initial wet weight of a freshly laid egg, recorded under controlled captive conditions, is approximately 74 grams [Ww0 = approximately 74 grams]. This delay between fledging and puberty allows for the completion of somatic growth and the accumulation of the physiological reserves necessary to support future reproductive effort.

The Jackal buzzard exhibits a typical annual reproductive schedule characterized by a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], a modest frequency that aligns with the species' relatively large body size and extended developmental periods. This extended lifespan, coupled with the delayed age at first reproduction and the small clutch size, paints a picture of a species with a slow life-history pace.
